prompt: Some cities have made all public transport free to use, paying for it through taxation instead of fares. Do you think this is a positive or negative development?
essay:
A small number of cities have abolished fares on their buses, trams and trains, funding the whole system from taxation instead. I regard this as a positive development overall, although its success depends heavily on how the lost fare income is replaced.

The strongest argument for free travel is a social one. Fares take a far larger share of a low income than of a high one, so for cleaners, carers and students the cost of reaching work or college can decide whether a job or a course is worth to take at all. Removing fares turns public transport into a genuinely universal service, in the same way as a public library or a pavement. There are practical gains too: boarding is quicker when nobody has to buy a ticket, and the considerable expense of selling and checking tickets simply disappears.

There is also an environmental case. If travelling by bus costs nothing, some drivers will be persuaded to leave their cars at home, which reduces both emissions and the demand for parking in the city centre. Critics respond that a free service will soon become overcrowded, and that taxpayers who never use it are being asked to subsidise those who do. The first objection is serious, since a crowded and unreliable bus is not attractive at any price. The second is weaker, because people who never drive already pay through their taxes for roads they do not use.

For these reasons I believe free public transport is a positive step, but only when the city increases its spending on the network rather than simply redistributing it. If abolishing fares leads to fewer buses running less often, the people it was meant to help will be left with a service that is free and yet far less useful.
title: Making public transport free
